newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage-takers chant their defiance.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage-takers chant their defiance.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 73 hostages in Lima chanted their defiance on Friday after President Alberto Fujimori threatened to wipe out their group once the 38-day standoff is over.

"Long live freedom," the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels could be heard chanting in the besieged residence of the Japanese ambassador to Peru as dawn broke and a fine white fog enveloped Lima.

The rebels also sang along for several minutes to what appeared to be a recording of a revolutionary song, the words to which could not be clearly heard despite their efforts to broadcast the event by megaphone. The singing and chanting brought a curious Peruvian policeman to the gate of the house, where he peered inside, but there was no other response from the security forces surrounding the house.

Fujimori, visiting La Paz in neighbouring Bolivia on Thursday, ratcheted up the psychological pressure on the hostage-takers, warning that he intended to wipe out the MRTA after the crisis. "We are looking for the total eradication of the group in the region," he said.

Speaking to reporters during a brief visit with Bolivia's President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada, Fujimori said he would not let up in his fight against rebel groups in Peru. "There is no going back. There are still isolated groups ... this government is going to hunt them down," he said.

Fujimori, whose younger brother Pedro is among the captives, has built much of his popular support on an aggressive fight against the MRTA and the larger and bloodier Maoist Shining Path rebel group. Local analysts say his efforts have reduced the MRTA to less than 250 active members.

Fujimori's tone underlined police tactics over the last few days stepping up pressure on the rebels in the residence. On Thursday four carpenters escorted by police boarded up one of the compound's two entrances and a small hole in the wall used by service staff, leaving only the entrance used by Red Cross workers, mediators and freed captives.
A police helicopter has also flown over the residence several times.
The MRTA has responded to the government's latest moves on the Internet, slamming Fujimori as a "dictator" whose security forces were preparing to storm the residence.

In a communique carried on its web home page, it said police activities around the diplomatic compound were "provocations that seek a pretext to justify military intervention ... We ask for the families, the press, human rights organisations and national and international solidarity to help prevent this massacre we warn of."
The roughly 15 rebels in the house are armed with assault rifles and grenade launchers and have mined and booby-trapped the compound against possible attack.

Though both sides have said they were willing to sit down to discuss a peaceful end to the crisis, Fujimori has ruled out starting talks until the rebels drop their demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
The rebels have said there is no point in talking unless that demand is on the agenda.

The MRTA originally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a cocktail party at the residence on Dec. 17. They freed most of them in what they called "goodwill gestures," keeping those they consider the best bargaining chips including two Peruvian government ministers, generals, security chiefs, about two dozen Japanese businessmen, and diplomats and ambassadors from Bolivia and Japan.
